𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗮 𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗮. The stock market is down around 𝟯𝟬%, the worst among major markets. MSCI is weighing a downgrade over governance and transparency. The rupiah crossed 𝟭𝟴,𝟬𝟬𝟬 to the dollar, and billions in portfolio money have left the country.

𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝘆𝗲𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗸𝗲𝗽𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴. 𝗨𝗦𝗗 𝟱𝟳 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 was realised in the first half, half of it foreign, and FDI grew 𝟮𝟳% year on year in the third quarter.
Portfolio money reacts to headlines. This year even gold, the classic safe haven, fell more than 𝟮𝟬% from its January record in a matter of days. Direct investment, the kind that builds hotels, factories and jobs, looks twenty years ahead. The real question is where it goes, and what it builds.

Tourism already generates 𝟰.𝟴% 𝗼𝗳 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗮'𝘀 𝗚𝗗𝗣. That's more than palm oil (around 3.5%) and about twice real estate (around 2.4%). Only mining, oil and gas included, is clearly bigger, at 8.8%, and it shrank last year. Yet tourism receives 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝟰% 𝗼𝗳 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁, and around three quarters of that still lands in Jakarta and Bali. The government's target is for tourism to reach 𝟴% 𝗼𝗳 𝗚𝗗𝗣 𝗯𝘆 𝟮𝟬𝟰𝟱.

The next markets are already visible: Lombok and Mandalika, Labuan Bajo, Lake Toba, Likupang. Visits to 𝗟𝗼𝗺𝗯𝗼𝗸 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗚𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘄 𝟳𝟮%. These destinations are poised to outgrow the national median, if access, infrastructure and the national masterplan deliver together.

One caution: tourism investment grew 𝟭𝟲.𝟲% in the first half, while international arrivals grew only 𝟱.𝟳%. Capital is arriving 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 than foreign visitors. Underwrite accordingly, and price the currency: revenue comes in rupiah, even when expectations are set in dollars.
This is a market for 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝘄𝗲𝗹𝗹-𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹. Fifteen years in investment management have taught me to ask six questions before any commitment:

→ 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 exactly to deploy?
→ 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀, 𝘀𝗲𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴?
→ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀 are really being underwritten?
→ What is the 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸-𝗮𝗱𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻, not just the headline IRR?
→ How will it be 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱?
→ Who 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹𝘀 it, and how do you 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘁?

In Indonesia, most of those answers must be decided before the day the company is incorporated.

Part One of my analysis for My Lombok Magazine is in the comments.

Turning Renewable Energy Opportunities into Bankable Investments
 
On 3 September 2026, the AMO team joined IndoEBTKE ConEx 2026 at JIExpo Kemayoran, Jakarta. Organized by Masyarakat Energi Terbarukan Indonesia (METI) and Masyarakat Konservasi dan Efisiensi Energi Indonesia (MASKEEI), the event brought together key stakeholders to exchange ideas on Indonesia's renewable energy and energy efficiency landscape.
This year's discussions came at an important time, as Indonesia moves forward with its 100 GW solar PV ambition and explores the next steps for B50 and E10 biofuel blending.
 
Representing AMO, Tony Nugroho, an energy investment expert in Indonesia, joined as one of the speakers at GGGI's breakout session, "Promoting Innovative Financing Mechanisms and Derisking for Financing Decentralized Renewable Energy in Indonesia."
 
Drawing on AMO's ongoing work with GGGI, Tony shared insights into why decentralized renewable energy projects—typically smaller projects spread across multiple locations—often face challenges in securing financing.
AMO's preliminary findings highlight four potential approaches to help unlock investment:
1. Standardizing contracts to simplify project assessment and improve bankability.
2. Strengthening borrower and project data to build lender confidence and support informed financing decisions.
3. Developing intermediary lending mechanisms to help channel financing to smaller renewable energy projects.
4. Creating diversified asset portfolios by combining projects across anchor users, off-taker types, and technologies to spread credit risks across locations.

Beyond the breakout session, the AMO team also exchanged perspectives with industry participants on emerging renewable energy opportunities and financing challenges. Several key insights stood out:
1. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is gaining traction. Discussions highlighted potential supply opportunities for international airlines and the prospect of a 1% blending requirement for domestic airlines.
2. Biofuel expansion continues to face financing and supply challenges. B50 remains dependent on CPO export levies, while E10 faces constraints related to domestic ethanol supply and limited subsidy support.
3. Banks are showing growing interest in renewable energy. Discussions highlighted state-owned banks' willingness to finance projects backed by experienced sponsors, alongside examples of private banks providing non-recourse financing to solar PV developers.
4. Rooftop solar remains a promising market. Evolving market arrangements and the implementation of MEMR Regulation No. 2/2024 will play an important role in shaping future growth.

We thank GGGI for the opportunity to contribute to the discussion, as well as METI and MASKEEI. AMO looks forward to translating these market insights into practical financing solutions that can help accelerate Indonesia's clean energy transition.

Built NoteSpace, a full-stack notes and revision workspace designed around a warm, editorial monograph aesthetic rather than cluttered note-taking tools.
Over the past few iterations, I focused on both architecture andhands-on polish:
Frontend (React + Vite): Crafted a 3-pane workspace (navigation & folders, searchable note stream, and distraction-free writing canvas) with Instrument Serif, Plus Jakarta Sans, and JetBrains Mono, backed by self-contained ns-* CSS styling and reliable state/routing flows.
Authentication & Role Access: Built Login/Register flows with role-based route protection (USER and ADMIN), quick demo credentials for testing, and a dedicatedAdmin Panel for user role management and workspace note auditing.
Backend & Persistence: Wired Node.js, Express, and MongoDB Atlas for real user accounts, notes, folders, search, and trash/restore workflows.
Debugging UI lockouts, aligning frontend props with auth context arguments, and making every button and route behave predictably taught me a lot about how small state and routing mismatches affect real user experience.
Would love feedback from fellow developers and builders—what features or workflows do you value most in a daily notes or study app?

Turning Renewable Energy Opportunities into Bankable Investments
 
On 3 September 2026, the AMO team joined IndoEBTKE ConEx 2026 at JIExpo Kemayoran, Jakarta. Organized by Masyarakat Energi Terbarukan Indonesia (METI) and Masyarakat Konservasi dan Efisiensi Energi Indonesia (MASKEEI), the event brought together key stakeholders to exchange ideas on Indonesia's renewable energy and energy efficiency landscape.
This year's discussions came at an important time, as Indonesia moves forward with its 100 GW solar PV ambition and explores the next steps for B50 and E10 biofuel blending.
 
Representing AMO, Tony Nugroho, an energy investment expert in Indonesia, joined as one of the speakers at GGGI's breakout session, "Promoting Innovative Financing Mechanisms and Derisking for Financing Decentralized Renewable Energy in Indonesia."
 
Drawing on AMO's ongoing work with GGGI, Tony shared insights into why decentralized renewable energy projects—typically smaller projects spread across multiple locations—often face challenges in securing financing.
AMO's preliminary findings highlight four potential approaches to help unlock investment:
1. Standardizing contracts to simplify project assessment and improve bankability.
2. Strengthening borrower and project data to build lender confidence and support informed financing decisions.
3. Developing intermediary lending mechanisms to help channel financing to smaller renewable energy projects.
4. Creating diversified asset portfolios by combining projects across anchor users, off-taker types, and technologies to spread credit risks across locations.

Beyond the breakout session, the AMO team also exchanged perspectives with industry participants on emerging renewable energy opportunities and financing challenges. Several key insights stood out:
1. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is gaining traction. Discussions highlighted potential supply opportunities for international airlines and the prospect of a 1% blending requirement for domestic airlines.
2. Biofuel expansion continues to face financing and supply challenges. B50 remains dependent on CPO export levies, while E10 faces constraints related to domestic ethanol supply and limited subsidy support.
3. Banks are showing growing interest in renewable energy. Discussions highlighted state-owned banks' willingness to finance projects backed by experienced sponsors, alongside examples of private banks providing non-recourse financing to solar PV developers.
4. Rooftop solar remains a promising market. Evolving market arrangements and the implementation of MEMR Regulation No. 2/2024 will play an important role in shaping future growth.

We thank GGGI for the opportunity to contribute to the discussion, as well as METI and MASKEEI. AMO looks forward to translating these market insights into practical financing solutions that can help accelerate Indonesia's clean energy transition.
